newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Opel sees 1997 as tough on sales, profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Opel sees 1997 as tough on sales, profit.

text.p: Adam Opel AG, the German unit of U.S. carmaker General Motors Corp, said on Thursday its 1996 sales rose 9.3 percent to 28.3 billion marks ($17.1 billion) but it expected weaker profits for the year due to stiff competition.

Opel said its 1996 profit would be at the high end of a range between 250 and 350 million marks but below the 1995 level of 363 million marks, hampered by higher dealer subsidies to spark sales but underpinned by a recovery in the mark.

The carmaker's 1995 profit was burdened by about 300 million marks in losses from currency market turbulence but Opel said it expected a double-digit contribution to 1996 profits from the mark's weakeness against many European rivals.
"We are satisfied with the results when viewed against the background of stiff competition and difficult industry conditions in 1996," Opel chief executive David Herman said.

Herman warned of ongoing tough times for 1997, saying Opel expected a lower rate of market growth and also pressure on sales, profit and vehicle deliveries, in part due to growing competition from importers, particularly from Korea.
But Opel said it would seek to expand its production and customer base despite tough times by teaming up with French carmaker Renault to build a series of light trucks.
The move marks Opel's return to a European market segment it had abandoned 20 years ago and that has since been dominated by rivals Volkswagen AG and Ford Motor Corp.
"It has been time for years to climb back into this market," Herman said.

The new trucks, which will have the Opel brand in Germany and Vauxhall in Britain but Renault elsewhere, will target the 2.5 tonne to 2.8 tonne weight class and will be introduced at the turn of the century.
In the interim, Opel will sell Renault trucks under GM's brands starting in 1998. Herman declined to provide financial details about the deal signed within the last six weeks.
Opel also said it was reviewing a potential joint venture with Japan's Suzuki Motor Corp to produce small cars but a deal has not yet been finalised.
Herman added that Opel would become in 1997 the first European carmaker to offer a three-cylinder engine, which will be first produced in the Corsa three-door car model.
In addition, Herman said Opel has hired about 150 new engineers to improve quality control, admitting recent trade reports of rising product defects were "partially accurate".

Herman also said Opel would intensify efforts to reduce costs and improve productivity but would not match a slew of hefty sales incentives offered by many Asian competitors -- with many selling vehicles at a loss to break into the market.
Few chances existed for Opel to raise vehicle prices due to rising competition in Germany where its market share slipped to 16 percent in 1996 from 16.7 percent in 1995.
"We will certainly not try to reduce the content, quality and price of our product to meet importers," Herman said, noting such offers could not last in the long-term.

German carmakers have not followed step behind carmakers such as Daewoo 7800.KS or Kia, who were part of a group of Korean firms that stepped up their share of the German market to a combined 1.4 percent in 1996 from one percent in 1995.

Although the carmakers pose no strong threat to German carmakers, Asian competitors are slowly siphoning off customers who are seeking low-cost vehicles that many carmakers must produce in massive volumes to make a profit.

Opel's 1996 revenues were boosted by strong sales of the Corsa as well as the popular Vectra saloon in addition to production of the Catera, a version of its Omega saloon, for export to the United States under the Cadillac brand.
Opel produced some 1.18 million units last year, up from 1.14 million in 1995. Production included about 876,000 vehicles and 306,000 parts at its factories.

But production in 1997 would likely remain steady since Opel said it expected new vehicle registrations in Germany during 1997 of 3.5 million to 3.6 million -- about stable with the 3.5 million new vehicles in Germany in 1996. West European registrations were also seen steady at almost 13 million.
($ = 1.653 German Marks)
